findings.headline: 2027-28 is the final budget for Newark and Sherwood in its current form; the council will cease to exist as a separate entity from 2028-29
findings.detail: The Local Government Reorganisation means the council merges into a new unitary authority from 2028-29 onwards. The budget strategy explicitly notes this is the last budget and that "it is not expected that the Community Plan will have any additional priorities added over the coming months, that would affect the budget position." Service continuity and planning assumptions transfer to the new authority.
findings.matters: For a lender, this signals uncertainty in governance and accountability from 2028-29. Financial performance and structural change create risk during a transition. Service plans and financial forecasts beyond 2027-28 rest on the new unitary's decisions, not this council's.
findings.figures: LGR effective date: 2028-29
findings.quote: 2027/28 will be the last created for Newark & Sherwood District Council. In previous years, budgets have been adjusted annually to include additional resources to fund new initiatives and updated priorities... As 2027/28 will be the final year of the Council in its current format, it is not expected that the Community Plan will have any additional priorities added over the coming months.

findings.headline: Pay award for 2026/27 remains unsettled with employees requesting significantly above the employer's 3.3% offer
findings.detail: The council has not yet received confirmation of the 2026/27 pay settlement for green and red book staff. The employer has offered 3.3% but employees are requesting substantially more. Budget was provisioned at 3.5% for 2025/26. The outcome affects both the current and next financial year's salary budgets.
findings.matters: Salary costs are the largest budget item. A settlement above the provisioned rate would force deficit-funding or require mid-year service reductions. Conversely, if the offer is accepted, it signals employee dissatisfaction during a major restructure.
findings.figures: Employer offer: 3.3%; prior year assumed: 3.5%; employee position: significantly higher
findings.quote: The Council are yet to receive information relating to the current years (2026/27) pay award for green and red book staff... The employer's offer for the current 2026/27 year is 3.3% with the employees' side asking for a significantly higher increase.

findings.headline: Funding deficits of £2.897m emerging by 2029/30 under current spending and grant assumptions
findings.detail: The MTFP shows funding shortfalls in 2028/29 (£93k) and 2029/30 (£2.897m), with the council noting these gaps reflect "reductions in grants and business rates income" rather than certainty of funding. The council acknowledges the gap but defers resolution to the new unitary authority expected to take over those years.
findings.matters: A £2.9m shortfall in the final year of the MTFP signals deteriorating grant funding and business rates. Even though the new unitary will assume responsibility, it indicates underlying income pressures that may carry forward into the merged authority.
findings.figures: 2028/29: £0.093m shortfall; 2029/30: £2.897m shortfall
findings.quote: The MTFP shows the gap in funding currently required to provide the same level of service as is currently provided by this Council. Also the current final year of the MTFP (2029/30) has assumptions of reductions in grants and business rates income, rather than the certainty of funding over the next three years.

findings.headline: Council shifting from an under-borrowed position to planned external borrowing to support cash flow
findings.detail: For years the council maintained an under-borrowed position against its Capital Financing Requirement, keeping reserves as a buffer. Now it plans to deploy reserves into capital projects, which means it must borrow externally to maintain day-to-day cash—a reversal of its historical capital financing model. The timing and rates for this borrowing have not yet been finalised.
findings.matters: This introduces ongoing debt service costs and locks in interest rate exposure at a time when rates remain elevated. It also signals reserves are being drawn down below prudent levels for cash liquidity.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document; relies on capital programme scale and reserve usage plans
findings.quote: The Council is proposing to borrow money in order to support its cash flow position. During previous financial years, decisions regarding capital expenditure have been taken to utilise internal resources and maintain an under borrowed position... This will mean that cash backed by these reserves will be utilised, hence there is a need to borrow money to ensure that the Council has cash at hand to service its day-to-day costs.

findings.headline: Council funding ongoing restructure costs from reserves rather than from within budgets
findings.detail: The LGR restructuring costs of £273,987 in 2026/27 and an additional £16,384 in 2027/28 are being funded by reserves set aside in 2025/26. This breaches the stated reserves policy (Appendix B), which requires reserves not to be used to support ongoing general fund expenditure. The council is instead supposed to use "other appropriate/earmarked reserves" first.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund ongoing salary and restructure costs rather than permanent efficiency savings signals the council cannot balance its budget within the spending envelope—a structural weakness that will persist once this one-time reserve is exhausted.
findings.figures: £273,987 (2026/27 LGR costs), £16,384 (2027/28 budget shortfall)
findings.quote: the additional budget required as a result of the restructure due to LGR in 2026/27 of £273,987 be funded by reserves set aside during 2025/26, and that the additional £16,384 to fund the 2027/28 budget be funded by the reserves set aside during 2025/26

findings.headline: £13.592m Housing Regeneration Loan increase in January 2026 with expected project delays
findings.detail: General Fund Loan facility increased materially for housing developments. The report notes 'certain developments were expected to require cash flow before the end of March 2026; however, these have since been delayed'. The loan has funded only £9.601m so far.
findings.matters: Material new borrowing commitment for housing. The delays in drawdown raise questions about project delivery and indicate the capital investments approved are not proceeding to schedule.
findings.figures: Loan facility increase £13.592m; actual spend against General Fund Loan £9.601m of £18.786m budget
findings.quote: the £13.592m increase in the Housing Regeneration Loan Facility was approved on 20 January 2026. At the time of approval, certain developments were expected to require cash flow before the end of March 2026; however, these have since been delayed

findings.headline: Major capital project delays: Stodman Street £0.928m and Yorke Drive £0.610m slippage
findings.detail: Stodman Street delayed by 'extensive delays in the national power cable diversions and other site complexities'. Yorke Drive regeneration delayed because 'Development Agreement was expected to be finalised in December 2025, however it requires a parent company guarantee'.
findings.matters: These are strategic regeneration projects. Delays indicate implementation and delivery risk, and raise questions about project management capability and external dependencies beyond the council's control.

findings.quote: Stodman Street – extensive delays in the national power cable diversions and other site complexities. (0.928)

findings.headline: Business Rates collection fund swung from £0.692m surplus to £0.469m deficit
findings.detail: In-year movement of £1.161m deterioration. The council's share of the deficit is £0.295m. This reduces the funding available for services in future years and adds to the Collection Fund deficit being recovered.
findings.matters: Business rates are core funding for the council. This swing indicates reduced business rate yield, either from reduced valuations or appeals, which is a permanent funding pressure.
findings.figures: In-year deficit £1.161m; year-end position swung from +£0.692m to -£0.469m; council share £0.295m
findings.quote: The in-year deficit on the Business Rates account was £1.161m, which changed the overall position from a surplus of £0.692m at 1 April 2025 to a deficit of £0.469m at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: HRA tenant arrears impairment provision increased £0.207m to £0.698m
findings.detail: Total HRA impaired debtor estimates rose from £0.491m to £0.698m. Current tenant arrears impairments specifically increased from £0.091m to £0.170m. This represents growing write-offs for non-payment of rent.
findings.matters: Growing provision for tenant arrears indicates rent collection is deteriorating. This directly threatens HRA revenue and is a leading indicator of financial stress in the housing service.
findings.figures: Total HRA impaired estimates: £0.491m → £0.698m; Current tenant arrears: £0.091m → £0.170m
findings.quote: HRA – Impaired Estimates on Debtors (0.491) 0.061 (0.268) (0.698)

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account operating deficit of £0.243m in 2025/26
findings.detail: The HRA before appropriations to reserves closed with a £0.243m deficit. While reserves cover this, it indicates the housing service is loss-making rather than self-sustaining from rental income. The variance deteriorated from the prior report.
findings.matters: Housing revenue accounts are designed to be self-financing from rental income and should break even. A deficit signals either inadequate rents or cost control issues, both of which are concerns for service sustainability.
findings.figures: £0.243m deficit; HRA expenditure £26.232m revised budget vs £25.555m outturn
findings.quote: The financial outturn position to 31 March 2026 for the HRA before appropriations to reserves is a deficit of £0.243m.

findings.paper_title: 08.07.26 Going Concern Status of the Council
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will dissolve the Council into a unitary authority on 1 April 2028
findings.detail: Newark and Sherwood District Council will cease to exist in 2028 when Nottinghamshire local government reorganises into unitary authorities. Three proposals are under consideration with a decision expected in July 2026. The paper states functions will continue under the new authority, but the specific terms of transition and treatment of existing borrowing have not yet been determined.
findings.matters: A lender with outstanding debt must understand how reorganisation will affect debt servicing obligations and which authority assumes responsibility for existing borrowing. Restructurings create transition risk until terms are finalised.
findings.figures: Restructure effective date: 1 April 2028; three proposals submitted; decision expected July 2026
findings.quote: Whilst this will see the closure of Newark and Sherwood District Council, the functions and services will continue to be provided by the newly created unitary authority, and hence this does not affect the going concern status of this authority.

findings.paper_title: 08.07.26 Going Concern Status of the Council
findings.headline: Capital programme significantly underspent with 74% of variance from lending to Arkwood subsidiary
findings.detail: The capital programme approved at £36.892m was only 66% spent (£24.439m outturn) with a £12.496m underspend attributed to project delays. Three-quarters of this underspend (~£9.2m) relates to the planned loan facility to Arkwood Developments Ltd, the Council's wholly owned subsidiary, indicating that subsidiary projects are not progressing as planned.
findings.matters: Persistent capital programme underperformance and specifically stalled lending to a council-owned subsidiary signals difficulty delivering development projects or potential issues within the subsidiary, both affecting council finances and strategic priorities.
findings.figures: £36.892m approved capital programme; £24.439m outturn; £12.496m underspend; 74% relates to Arkwood loan
findings.quote: The outturn performance was £ 24.439m which represents an under-spend, due to delays in capital projects, of £12.496m. 74% of this variance relates to the loan facility with the Council's wholly owned subsidiary Arkwood Developments Ltd.

findings.paper_title: 08.07.26 Going Concern Status of the Council
findings.headline: Medium Term Financial Plan requires reserve drawdown in final two years to achieve balance
findings.detail: The approved MTFP to 2029/30 shows a balanced budget overall but requires use of the MTFP Reserve in years 2029/30 to balance due to uncertainty over Government funding. This indicates underlying funding pressure that the council will need to manage through reserve depletion rather than ongoing income.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether a council's budget balance depends on continued reserve depletion. This signals structural funding challenges that will erode financial resilience in the outer years.
findings.figures: 4-year MTFP to 2029/30; MTFP Reserve use required in final two years
findings.quote: over the four-year period to 20 29/30 the Council has a balanced budget . However, t his is does require the use of the Council's MTFP Reserve within the final two years . This is due to uncertainty over Government funding in the final year of the MTFP

findings.headline: Major projects delivery risk newly flagged with target score still to be confirmed
findings.detail: A new strategic risk (SR605) has been created specifically for 'Failure to deliver or sufficiently advance approved capital projects within the Council's Capital Programme and Community Plan prior to mandated funding deadlines and/or the end of Newark & Sherwood District Council.' The target risk score is still 'to be confirmed at next review', indicating uncertainty about the scale of this risk.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage or project failure impacts financial forecasting, reserve management, and the council's ability to deliver planned capital investment.
findings.figures: New risk SR605 introduced; Capital programme referenced; Grant funding agreements mentioned as controls
findings.quote: Failure to deliver or sufficiently advance approved capital projects within the Council's Capital Programme and Community Plan prior to mandated funding deadlines and/or the end of Newark & Sherwood District Council.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation introduced as new strategic risk, currently above council target
findings.detail: Newark & Sherwood is undergoing reorganisation into a new unitary authority. This is now a formal strategic risk because of stated pressures on workforce capacity, operational resilience, and the ability to maintain business-as-usual during transition. The risk score is 'Not yet at SLT target score'. Key trigger events include loss of key staff, disruption to critical services, and governance uncertainties during the shadow authority phase.
findings.matters: Organisational restructuring creates material risk to financial controls, service delivery, staffing stability, and the council's ability to manage debt during a critical transition period.
findings.figures: May 2027 elections for shadow authority mentioned; Vesting day implied; Reorganisation of nine councils into one unitary
findings.quote: To ensure smooth transition maintaining effective business as usual (BAU) delivery while implementing significant change.

findings.headline: HRA financial sustainability risk not at SLT target score
findings.detail: The council's Housing Revenue Account risk score remains static but is explicitly noted as 'Not yet at SLT target score', meaning it sits above the council's own acceptable threshold. The HRA finances are a major revenue stream for the council, and this indicates the housing account is carrying more financial risk than management considers tolerable.
findings.matters: HRA financial stress directly affects the council's overall financial position and debt servicing capacity, both key lending concerns.
findings.figures: Current risk score marked above target score for SR602; Council owns and manages housing stock through HRA
findings.quote: Risk score has remained static. Not yet at SLT target score.

findings.headline: Capital programme will require £12.784m of new borrowing, which attracts Minimum Revenue Provision charges to revenue budget over asset lives.
findings.detail: The four-year capital programme totals £48.093m, of which £14.925m is grant-funded and £13.123m comes from the council's own resources. The remaining £12.784m will be financed by borrowing. This borrowing attracts mandatory annual Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charges to the revenue budget, calculated using the asset life method. Capital projects show scheduling delays: the Clipstone Holdings Centre development was moved from 2026/27 to 2027/28.
findings.matters: Capital borrowing creates long-term revenue commitments that will constrain future budgets; project delivery delays create uncertainty about when MRP charges will materialise.
findings.figures: £12.784m borrowing required; total capital programme £48.093m; grant funding £14.925m; council resources £13.123m
findings.quote: Borrowing is the balancing figure for the capital expenditure at £12.784m. This type of financing attracts a charge to revenue called the Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) calculated using the asset life method

findings.headline: Employee pay is budgeted for only 3.5% increase but comprises 54% of controllable spend, creating exposure if pay awards exceed assumption.
findings.detail: Employee costs represent 54% of the council's controllable service expenditure for 2026/27. The MTFP assumes a 3.5% pay award for 2026/27 and 3.5% for each subsequent year. The Section 151 Officer explicitly warns that if actual pay awards exceed this and employee cost reductions elsewhere are unavailable, additional costs would need to be funded from council reserves. The council applies a 7.5% vacancy provision.
findings.matters: With over half the budget tied to employee costs and limited scope to cut non-pay spending, the council is highly exposed to pay inflation that could force earlier reserve drawdown than planned.
findings.figures: 54% of controllable service expenditure; 3.5% assumed pay award; 7.5% vacancy provision (actual 2024/25: 8.32%)
findings.quote: If the 2026/27 pay award is agreed at a higher rate than the 3.5% increase in basic pay assumed, and if reductions in employee costs elsewhere cannot offset the increase in pay award costs, the additional costs unbudgeted for will need to be funded from council reserves.

findings.headline: Council's tax base is 159 band D properties below government settlement assumptions, creating structural underfunding in each year.
findings.detail: The government settlement assumes a 2026/27 tax base of 43,431.21 equivalent band D properties with a £204.54 band D charge, but the council forecasts 42,720.66 and £198.60. This 158.76 property shortfall means the council will raise less council tax income than the settlement assumes. The document explicitly states this variance carries forward into 2027/28 and 2028/29, compounding the structural gap.
findings.matters: The council is financially underfunded relative to what government settlement formulae assume it can raise locally, meaning council tax cannot fill the gap that central funding fails to cover.
findings.figures: 158.76 band D properties shortfall; £204.54 (government assumption) vs £198.60 (council forecast) band D charge; £8.883m government assumption vs actual lower income
findings.quote: The Governments assumption of £8.883m with a band D charge of £204.54 means that their expectation of tax base would be 43,431.21. This is 158.76 equivalent band D properties more than the Councils forecast.

findings.headline: Council will draw down £2.706m from reserves in 2029/30 to balance the budget, the first year of structural deficit in the MTFP.
findings.detail: The council's MTFP shows balanced budgets for 2026/27-2028/29, but 2029/30 reveals a £2.706m funding shortfall that will be met by using reserves. The MTFP reserve is expected to close at £8.925m in March 2026 and decline to £6.219m by March 2030. The council notes this shortfall coincides with creation of the new unitary authority, which will inherit the underlying funding challenge.
findings.matters: This signals when the council exhausts sustainable funding and becomes reliant on reserve depletion to meet its budget, reducing financial flexibility and increasing borrowing risk.
findings.figures: £2.706m shortfall in 2029/30; MTFP reserve £8.925m (March 2026) declining to £6.219m (March 2030)
findings.quote: As can be seen from the table, the Council has sufficient funding over the next three years to fund service provision, whilst in the fourth year it is expecting to need to take £2.706m out of reserves to balance the budget.

findings.paper_title: 05.03.26 - Medium Term Financial Plan 26-27 to 2029-30 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Homelessness Fund growing from £671k to £2.0m over the planning period
findings.detail: The Homelessness Fund nearly triples from £671k in March 2025 to £2.0m by March 2030, indicating the council is setting aside increasing resources for homelessness pressure. The fund reaches £1.4m by March 2028 alone.
findings.matters: Rapid growth in homelessness reserves suggests either rising demand the council anticipates, or a service that is underfunded in base budgets and being supported from reserves

findings.paper_title: 05.03.26 - Medium Term Financial Plan 26-27 to 2029-30 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Total General Fund and Capital Reserves declining by 55% over five years
findings.detail: Combined revenue and capital reserves fall from £50.2m in March 2025 to £22.3m by March 2030. This sustained, significant depletion reduces the council's financial resilience and capacity to absorb unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion at this scale is a material change to the council's financial strength and indicates either planned use of reserves or unmatched spending to income
findings.figures: Total General Fund Revenue and Capital Reserves: £50,203,561 (2025) to £22,318,598 (2030)

findings.paper_title: 05.03.26 - Medium Term Financial Plan 26-27 to 2029-30 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Change Management/Capital Fund being completely exhausted by 2029
findings.detail: The council's Change Management/Capital Fund stands at £13.8m in March 2025 and is projected to reach zero by March 2029. By March 2028 it is already down to £858k. After exhaustion, the council will have no dedicated reserve for change initiatives or capital projects.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can fund capital investment and improvement after this reserve is gone, and whether exhaustion signals planned transformation spending or inadequate funding for recurrent pressures

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan_Cllr Kellas Amendment
findings.headline: Council to draw £0.285m from reserves over two years to fund a Council Tax rise reduction
findings.detail: The amendment proposes reducing planned Council Tax increases in years 3–4 of the MTFP period. This voluntary reduction would cost the council approximately £0.285m over the two financial years. The amendment proposes this be funded through drawdown from the Medium-Term Financial Plan Reserve, which currently stands at £6.219m at the end of the MTFP period.
findings.matters: A lender and finance director need to understand how the council is managing its reserves and whether it is spending them to offset difficult revenue decisions. Discretionary reserve drawdown reduces the financial buffer available for unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: £0.285m over two years; MTFP Reserve balance £6.219m
findings.quote: The proposed reduction in Council Tax in years 2028/29 and 2029/30 would cost the Council circa £0.285m over the course of the two financial years. This could be funded through the Medium-Term Financial Plan Reserve.

findings.headline: £556k funding gap for discretionary spending to be met from MTFP Reserve, leaving £6.219m balance at end of period
findings.detail: Combined cost of council tax reduction (£400k over MTFP) plus ward fund (£156k over MTFP) totals £556k, funded from reserves rather than recurrent income. The MTFP Reserve balance is stated as £6.219m at the end of the planning period.
findings.matters: Funding discretionary spending from reserves rather than recurrent income warrants monitoring. While a £6.2m balance appears adequate, a pattern of reserve drawdown for current commitments can signal emerging unsustainability.
findings.figures: £0.556m total cost over MTFP; MTFP Reserve balance £6.219m at end of period
findings.quote: Therefore, the total financial implication of the proposed amendment would cost the Council £0.556m over the life of the Medium-Term Financial Plan, which could be funded through the Medium-Term Financial Plan Reserve. The balance on the MTFP Reserve (as identified on page 39 of the Budget Book) at the end of the MTFP period stands at £6.219m.

findings.headline: New Members Ward Fund allocating £1,000 per councillor (£39,000 total annually) for discretionary distribution to local causes
findings.detail: The amendment adds discretionary spending whereby each of the 39 council members receives £1,000 to allocate to charities, community groups and public bodies in their wards. Over the MTFP period this costs £0.156m.
findings.matters: This represents discretionary allocation of public funds by individual councillors. It signals governance approach to spending and the council's latitude to create new programs beyond statutory services.
findings.figures: £1,000 per member; £39,000 annual cost; £0.156m over MTFP
findings.quote: Members Ward Fund, added to the base budget for 2026/27, whereby each individual member is allocated a sum of £1,000 (£39,000 in total) to support charities, community groups and public bodies working within their wards for the benefit of residents.

findings.headline: Council tax reduction of 1.12% instead of freeze, reducing income by £400k over the MTFP period
findings.detail: The amendment proposes reducing council tax by 1.12% for 2026/27 rather than holding it flat as in the base budget. This costs £0.096m in 2026/27 and £0.400m over the full Medium-Term Financial Plan period — a deliberate choice to reduce council income.
findings.matters: Most councils freeze or raise council tax under current financial pressure; a reduction signals either exceptional financial strength or political priority overriding fiscal caution. A lender needs to understand which.
findings.figures: 1.12% reduction; £0.096m in 2026/27; £0.400m over MTFP
findings.quote: The cost of the proposed reduction in Council Tax by 1.12% would be £0.096m in 2026/27. The impact over the life of the Medium-Term Financial Plan would be £0.400m.

findings.headline: The council is maintaining an under-borrowed position, betting that long-term interest rates will fall from current elevated levels (5.38-5.40% for 10-year PWLB borrowing).
findings.detail: Rather than borrowing now to fund capital needs, the council is using reserves as 'internal borrowing'. The strategy document states this approach is 'prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels'. However, if rates do not fall as forecast, the council will borrow the required £43m at current high rates, materially increasing debt costs.
findings.matters: This is a material interest rate bet. With shrinking reserves and rising debt requirements, higher-than-forecast borrowing costs would strain affordability. A lender would be concerned if rates remain elevated when the council is forced to borrow.
findings.figures: 10-year PWLB Certainty Rate 5.38% (01/04/2025), 5.53% (30/09/2025), averaging 5.40% for the period; 25-year average 6.11%
findings.quote: This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels once prevailing inflation concerns are addressed by tighter near-term monetary policy.

findings.headline: HRA borrowing capacity has dropped 73% in one year, to only £2.3m additional capacity by 2026/27, due to Interest Cover Ratio constraints.
findings.detail: The council uses an Interest Cover Ratio of 1.50 to set HRA borrowing limits. Additional capacity was £8.5m in 2025/26 but falls to £2.7m in 2026/27 and £2.3m in 2028/29. With the HRA CFR growing from £109m to £143m, this tight constraint leaves little room for error if rental income disappoints or operating costs rise.
findings.matters: The HRA is a major part of the council's balance sheet (40% of total CFR). Constrained HRA borrowing severely limits the council's overall flexibility and means minimal buffer if housing operations underperform.
findings.quote: the maximum additional debt capacity set is £2.308m in order to maintain affordability in each financial year

findings.headline: The council's capital financing requirement is growing 48% to £198.9m, requiring minimum additional borrowing of £43m over the forecast period.
findings.detail: The CFR (underlying borrowing need) is rising from £146.7m to £217.0m due to the capital programme, while external borrowing actually falls from £108.9m to £85.7m. The council explicitly acknowledges it 'will be required to borrow up to a minimum of an additional £43m over the forecast period'. This new borrowing will occur at current elevated rates (10-year PWLB at 5.38-5.40%).
findings.matters: Material increase in borrowing requirements on top of existing debt raises leverage and debt-servicing costs. A lender would be concerned whether the council can afford higher interest costs as rates remain elevated.
findings.figures: CFR £146.7m (2024/25) → £198.9m (2026/27) → £217.0m (2028/29); external borrowing £108.9m → £100.8m → £85.7m; minimum additional borrowing £43m
findings.quote: The Council has an increasing CFR due to the proposed capital programme and diminishing investments and will therefore be required to borrow up to a minimum of an additional £43m over the forecast period.

findings.headline: Usable reserves will fall by 51% over four years while capital investment grows, from £68.5m to £33.2m.
findings.detail: The council is using reserves to fund capital spending, with Major Repairs Reserve alone drawn down by £20.2m in 2026/27. By 2028/29, usable reserves will be less than half their current level. This erodes the financial cushion available to absorb unexpected costs or service disruptions.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's financial flexibility and resilience. A lender would be concerned that the council is simultaneously expanding its capital programme and eroding its financial buffer.
findings.figures: Usable reserves £68.5m (2024/25) declining to £33.2m (2028/29); Major Repairs Reserve drawdown £20.2m (2026/27), £6.1m (2027/28), £1.7m (2028/29)

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account financing costs at 30.69% of net revenue stream in 2026/27; General Fund at negative 10.56% but tracking worse
findings.detail: HRA financing costs (interest, depreciation, debt repayment net of income) are projected at £9.894m against net revenue of £32.224m — a ratio of 30.69%. This burden is high and makes the HRA vulnerable to any revenue pressure. The General Fund has negative financing costs (-10.56% in 2026/27, meaning investment income exceeds borrowing costs), but this position deteriorates to -13.62% in 2027/28 and -18.34% in 2028/29, driven by falling investment income as reserves deplete.
findings.matters: HRA at 30.69% is a stress indicator if rent collection or occupancy declines, or if maintenance costs rise. The GF's apparent 'negative cost' is an accounting artefact of holding investments; as reserves fall, this advantage evaporates, and the GF will face actual interest costs in the forward years.
findings.figures: HRA 2026/27: interest £4.281m, depreciation £6.364m, MRR contributions -£700k, investment income -£51k. Total £9.894m. Net revenue stream £32.224m (implied). GF financing costs 2026/27: -1.458m on revenue stream of 13.810m (net revenue).
findings.quote: Proportion of financing costs to net revenue stream ... Housing Revenue Account Interest Payable 4,281 ... Proportion of net revenue stream 30.69%

findings.headline: Investment holdings declining sharply: treasury investments falling from £54.975m to £38.979m over one year
findings.detail: Short-term treasury investments are forecast to drop from £43.980m (2025/26) to £27.285m (2026/27). This 38% fall in liquid cash reserves is expected to continue, with holdings projected at £37.089m by 2027/28 and £33.716m by 2028/29. This mirrors the capital spend spike: reserves are being deployed for capex funding.
findings.matters: Declining investment income will hit the General Fund revenue budget if interest rates normalize downward. The council is currently receiving £2.598m investment income on GF, which offsets its borrowing costs; as reserves fall, this buffer shrinks. A lender needs visibility on cash and liquidity runway.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement projected to rise £24.8m in 2026/27, reaching £198.946m by year-end
findings.detail: The CFR (cumulative amount of past capital expenditure still financed by debt) increases from £173.959m (2025/26 forecast) to £198.946m (2026/27). This is driven by £28.839m new borrowing, offset only by £3.044m HRA debt repayment and £807k General Fund MRP. The CFR continues rising to £213.221m in 2027/28 and £217.034m in 2028/29, suggesting the council is in a multi-year cycle of increasing leverage.
findings.matters: CFR growth signals the council is accumulating debt faster than it is repaying it. While the council has headroom (£98.135m under-borrowing against the CFR), the upward trajectory is important for long-term debt sustainability and future borrowing capacity.

findings.detail: The budget assumes 'Vacancy Factor and Notional Savings' of £2.017790m, up from £1.170m in the March estimate. This is 8.5% of total service budgets. These are savings the council expects to find but has not yet identified or allocated to particular services.
findings.matters: If these unidentified savings cannot be realised, the budget will not balance. A lender would want to know whether a council is balancing on firm plans or on assumptions.
findings.figures: £2,017,790; increase of £848,110 from March estimate
findings.quote: Vacancy Factor and Notional Savings (1,169,680) (2,017,790) (848,110)

findings.headline: Only first year of settlement is firm; years 2-3 indicative and subject to change before statutory confirmation
findings.detail: The government settlement is only statutory for 2026/27; figures for 2027/28 and 2028/29 are indicative and could change when formally announced. Business rates safety net also reduces from 100% (year 1) to 97% (year 2) to 92.5% (year 3), meaning only £3.843m guaranteed in 2027/28 (versus £3.961m assumed) and £3.739m in 2028/29 (versus £4.042m assumed).
findings.matters: Forecast years 2 and 3 rest on assumptions that may not hold; if government changes funding allocations or business rates perform worse than protected, funding gaps could widen materially beyond what is currently planned.
findings.figures: Business rates safety net: 100% year 1, 97% year 2, 92.5% year 3; Year 2 guaranteed funding £3.843m (vs £3.961m assumed); Year 3 guaranteed funding £3.739m (vs £4.042m assumed)
findings.quote: The 2026/27 settlement provides a three-year funding framework, but only the first year is statutory, with subsequent years remaining indicative and subject to change.

findings.headline: Arkwood Developments expected to contribute £1.1m but lacks detail on delivery or security
findings.detail: The council's wholly owned development company is expected to contribute at least £1.100m over the four-year period, but the document provides no detail on specific projects, development timelines, or how secure this income is. Multiple commercial strategy projects are also noted as not yet reflected in the MTFP or subject to trial/approval.
findings.matters: Development company returns are discretionary and market-dependent; without detail on the projects or delivery schedule, this £1.1m represents a significant forecast dependency with unclear probability of realisation.
findings.figures: Arkwood Developments expected contribution 2026/27-2029/30: at least £1.100m
findings.quote: The Council's wholly owned development company – Arkwood Developments Ltd are expected to make a financial contribution of at least £1.100m from 2026/27 to 2029/30.

findings.headline: Council tax income forecast understates government settlement assumptions by 158.76 band D equivalents
findings.detail: The government's provisional settlement assumes council tax income of £8.883m based on an assumed tax base of 43,431.21 band D equivalents, but the council forecasts a tax base 158.76 properties lower (42,720.66). This variance carries forward through years 2 and 3, meaning the council's actual council tax income will fall below government expectations.
findings.matters: Tax base forecasts affect both the council's own income and its position within the government funding formula; variance between forecast and actual income can widen funding gaps if not addressed.
findings.figures: Council tax income assumed by government: £8.883m; Council's forecast band D base: 42,720.66; Government assumption: 43,431.21 (variance of 158.76 properties)
findings.quote: The Governments assumption of £8.883m with a band D charge of £204.54 means that their expectation of tax base would be 43,431.21. This is 158.76 equivalent band D properties more than the Councils forecast.

findings.headline: Capital borrowing of £12.784m creates ongoing Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charges to revenue budget
findings.detail: The council plans to finance £12.784m of its £48.093m capital programme through borrowing (the rest comes from grants and internal resources). Borrowing commits the council to recurring MRP charges calculated over the asset life, compounding the revenue funding challenge in outer years when capital schemes come online.
findings.matters: Borrowing creates locked-in future revenue costs; with the council already facing a structural deficit in year 4, large capital borrowing commitments reduce flexibility and increase the revenue burden, particularly as MRP charges build over time.
findings.figures: Total capital programme 2026/27-2029/30: £48.093m; Financing by borrowing: £12.784m; External grants: £14.925m; Internal resources: £13.123m
findings.quote: Borrowing is the balancing figure for the capital expenditure at £12.784m. This type of financing attracts a charge to revenue called the Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) calculated using the asset life method

findings.headline: Pay award risk: employee costs are 54% of controllable expenditure but budget assumes only 3.5% annual growth
findings.detail: Employee costs comprise 54% of the council's controllable service expenditure. The MTFP budgets for 3.5% pay award annually, but if actual awards exceed this and offsetting savings cannot be found elsewhere, the shortfall will force additional draws on reserves. Year-on-year employee cost increases are large (£1.488m in 2027/28, £0.893m in 2028/29, £0.915m in 2029/30).
findings.matters: With over half of controllable spend committed to employee costs, there is limited room to offset pay award overruns through service reductions. Pay awards are often above inflation and difficult to forecast; this is a material risk to budget stability.
findings.figures: Employee costs as % of controllable expenditure: 54%; Assumed pay award: 3.5% per year; Employee cost increase 2027/28: £1.488m; 2028/29: £0.893m; 2029/30: £0.915m
findings.quote: If the 2026/27 pay award is agreed at a higher rate than the 3.5% increase in basic pay assumed, and if reductions in employee costs elsewhere cannot offset the increase in pay award costs, the additional costs unbudgeted for will need to be funded from council reserves.

findings.headline: MTFP reserve declining from £8.925m to £6.219m over the planning period
findings.detail: The council's earmarked MTFP reserve (specifically set aside to mitigate future funding pressures) is forecast to decline by 30% over four years, from £8.925m at end-March 2026 to £6.219m at end-March 2030. The fourth year draws £2.706m directly from this reserve to balance the budget.
findings.matters: Depleting financial reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs, demand shocks, or funding changes; the declining reserve trajectory limits the council's financial flexibility and resilience, particularly important given only year 1 of the settlement is certain.
findings.figures: MTFP reserve closing balance March 2026: £8.925m; forecast closing balance March 2030: £6.219m; utilisation 2026/27-2029/30: £2.706m
findings.quote: As per Appendix A the MTFP reserve is expected to have a closing balance at the end of March 2026 of £8.925m. As per table 5 above the proposed utilisation of balances from the MTFP reserve during 2026/27 to 2029/30 will leave a balance of £6.219m at the end of March 2030.

findings.headline: Structural funding gap of £2.706m emerges in 2029/30, forcing reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The council balances budgets for the first three years but faces a £2.706m shortfall in 2029/30 that must be covered by drawing reserves. This is the only year in the forecast where expenditure cannot be matched by predicted income and requires planned reserve use, indicating emerging structural deficit.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council can operate sustainably; structural deficits that require reserves in year 4 signal that future funding assumptions or spending levels are not sustainable, and the incoming unitary authority will inherit this gap.
findings.figures: Funding Shortfall prior to Mitigations 2029/30: £2.706m; Use of MTFP reserve in 2029/30: £2.706m
findings.quote: Funding Shortfall prior to Mitigations 0 0 0 2.706

findings.paper_title: 24.02.26 - Medium Term Financial Plan 26-27 to 2029-30 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Repairs and Renewals Fund depleted to zero by 2029, ending routine capital maintenance funding
findings.detail: The Repairs and Renewals Fund falls from £2.4m (2025) to zero by 2029, declining in each year before exhaustion. Once depleted, the council will have no dedicated reserve to fund routine asset repairs or renewals without budget reallocation or borrowing.
findings.matters: A council unable to fund repairs risks asset deterioration, emergency failures, and rising maintenance liabilities; this also signals future pressure to borrow for capital or divert revenue spending.

findings.paper_title: 24.02.26 - Medium Term Financial Plan 26-27 to 2029-30 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Homelessness Fund growing to £2m by 2030, tripling from 2025, with consistent annual increases
findings.detail: The Homelessness Fund grows from £671k (2025) to £2.02m (2030), increasing by £160–330k every year from 2027 onwards. This consistent growth is unusual against the backdrop of overall reserve decline and suggests the council expects homelessness demand to continue rising and is earmarking reserves to meet it.
findings.matters: Homelessness services are often underfunded by government grant; if the council is managing escalating demand by drawdown of reserves rather than sustainable funding, this is not a permanent solution and signals pressure on future budgets.

findings.paper_title: 24.02.26 - Medium Term Financial Plan 26-27 to 2029-30 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Change Management/Capital Fund depleted from £13.2m to zero by 2029, with £11m drawn in a single year
findings.detail: The council's Change Management/Capital Fund falls from £13.2m (2026) to £2.1m (2027)—a £11.1m reduction in one year—and reaches zero by 2029. This reserve appears to be financing transformation or capital initiatives that the council expects to be completed or paid for by 2029.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand whether the change programmes this fund supports will deliver promised savings; if they slip or fail, the council will lack the reserves to fund them and may need emergency borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 24.02.26 - Medium Term Financial Plan 26-27 to 2029-30 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Total reserves to fall from £50m to £22m—a 55% decline over five years, with sharpest drop between 2026 and 2027
findings.detail: General Fund Revenue and Capital Reserves are projected to drop from £50.2m (March 2025) to £22.3m (March 2030). The decline accelerates between 2026 and 2027, when reserves fall by £12.2m (from £44.8m to £32.6m) in a single year. This sustained depletion means the council's financial buffer will shrink substantially.
findings.matters: A lender depends on council reserves as evidence of financial resilience and ability to absorb spending shocks; a 55% reduction signals declining capacity to manage unexpected pressures without borrowing or service cuts.

findings.headline: The Change Management/Capital Fund, the council's largest reserve at £13.8m, is projected to reach zero by 2029.
findings.detail: This reserve collapses from £13.8m in 2025 to £2.1m by 2027 and £0 by 2029. This is the single largest planned drawdown in the reserve portfolio, suggesting significant one-time capital or reorganisation spending planned through 2029.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand what major capital projects or change programmes justify this spend-down, and whether those projects deliver the benefits needed to maintain the council's financial position after 2029.

findings.headline: The Homelessness Fund is projected to triple from £671k to £2.0m over five years, signalling sustained growth in homelessness spending.
findings.detail: The reserve grows every year without interruption, suggesting the council is planning for year-on-year increases in homelessness service costs. The fund grows from £671k in 2025 to £2.0m by 2030.
findings.matters: Growing homelessness demand indicates a structural service pressure that will consume an increasing share of the budget and may eventually require harder choices about service provision or taxation.

findings.headline: The Repairs and Renewals Fund will be completely exhausted by 2028–29, leaving no buffer for building maintenance.
findings.detail: This reserve, which typically funds essential maintenance and renewal of council assets, starts at £2.4m in 2025 and declines to £92k by 2028, reaching zero the following year. Councils usually maintain a repairs reserve to avoid emergency spending on property failures.
findings.matters: Depleting a maintenance reserve forces the council either to defer necessary building repairs or to find emergency funding for them, both of which indicate financial strain and create deferred-maintenance risk across the asset base.

findings.headline: Officers acknowledge weak understanding of income volumes and plan to develop better forecasting
findings.detail: Paragraph 3.66 states: "Officers plan to develop a more detailed understanding of the volumes of activity which underpin each of the Council's main income sources. This will allow the Council to more accurately model changes to expected activity levels, as well as increase assurance regarding the risks of such changes materialising." This is an implicit admission that current income forecasting lacks adequate granularity.
findings.matters: Income assumptions across fees and charges (£5.8m budgeted) and other sources are not yet modelled with sufficient detail. Future revisions could be significant if activity volumes diverge from assumptions.
findings.figures: Total budgeted fees and charges 2026/27: £5.8m (increase of £0.404m from 2025/26)
findings.quote: Officers plan to develop a more detailed understanding of the volumes of activity which underpin each of the Council's main income sources.

findings.headline: Council deliberately freezes Council Tax despite being permitted a 3% increase without referendum
findings.detail: Government permitted a 3% increase or £5 per Band D property without triggering referendum. Newark and Sherwood chose a full freeze, resulting in Band D charge of £198.60 (unchanged) and Band A charge of £132.40. This is an explicit constraint on available income.
findings.matters: A political choice to forego ~£257k in available tax revenue (3% of £8.59m). This narrows flexibility if other income sources underperform or costs exceed budget.
findings.figures: Band D: £198.60 (frozen); potential available increase 3% or £5 per property; foregone revenue estimated at ~£257k (3% × £8.593m)
findings.quote: The proposal within this paper is a Council Tax freeze for the 2026/27 financial year.

findings.headline: 2026/27 pay award not yet finalised; 1% overage against 3.5% budget would require £198k from reserves
findings.detail: The budget assumes a 3.5% pay award, but paragraph 3.62 notes "The National Joint Council (NJC) for Local Government Services' pay award for 2026/27 has not yet been finalised." If the award exceeds budget and cannot be offset by other savings, the difference must come from reserves.
findings.matters: A significant budget risk remains unresolved at the point this budget is proposed. Pay awards for local government are sector-wide and not controllable at council level. A 1% overage is material at £198k.
findings.figures: 1% pay award overage = £198,000 from reserves; 3.5% budgeted baseline
findings.quote: If the 2026/27 pay award agrees a more than 3.5% increase in basic pay, and if reductions in employee costs elsewhere cannot offset the increase in pay award costs, the additional costs unbudgeted for will need to be funded from council reserves.

findings.headline: Vacancy factor increased to 7.5% (from 5%), generating £817k savings on a budget assumption
findings.detail: The vacancy factor — the amount of pay budget assumed to remain unspent due to posts standing vacant — has been increased from 5% to 7.5% of total salary budget (£1.77m budgeted). This accounts for £816,820 of the £417,820 net budget reduction from March 2025 to February 2026. If posts are filled faster than assumed, the budget will face pressure.
findings.matters: A significant portion of the budget savings depends on higher vacancy assumptions. Recruitment pressure or service pressures forcing faster filling of posts would create unbudgeted cost.
findings.figures: 7.5% vacancy factor = £1,767,790; variance from previous assumption £816,820
findings.quote: 7.5% of the Council's total salary budget, or £1,767,790, has been budgeted to be saved from posts that remain vacant for a period of time before being filled.

findings.headline: Multiple income streams removed or reduced: asylum seekers (£75.5k), Homes for Ukraine grant (£148.8k), and Internal Drainage Board grant (partial loss)
findings.detail: Asylum Seeker income noted as "not due to receive any income in 2026/27"; Homes for Ukraine income loss because "this level of income is not expected to be received going forward as it is based on a fixed charge per house visit"; IDB grant only £158,000 budgeted (equivalent to 2025/26) despite cost increases of 40% since 2022/23 and receiving £239,690 support in 2023/24.
findings.matters: Income that was received in prior years is now removed from budget, representing permanent loss rather than allocation variation. These are primarily government-funded programmes being reduced or ceased.
findings.figures: Asylum Seekers £75,500 lost; Homes for Ukraine £148,780 lost; IDB grant reduction from £239,690 (2023/24) to £158,000 (2026/27)
findings.quote: Homes for Ukraine - Income previously received from Nottinghamshire County Council, this level of income is not expected to be received going forward as it is based on a fixed charge per house visit

findings.headline: Nottinghamshire Business Rates Pool dissolved after finding risks outweighed rewards
findings.detail: The pool conducted a review in January 2026 and determined it would be dissolved at the end of 2025/26. This removes the risk-sharing mechanism that previously buffered volatility in business rates collection across member authorities.
findings.matters: The council loses the protection of pooling arrangements and is now fully exposed to business rates collection volatility. The baseline safety net is now 100% (paragraph 3.19), but volatility above/below baseline is now the council's risk alone.
findings.figures: Pool dissolved decision made via Portfolio Holder decision 12 January 2026
findings.quote: The outcome of that review found that the risks outweighed the rewards and hence the Pool would be dissolved at the end of the 2025/26 financial year.

findings.headline: Business rates baseline reset removes all assumed growth income for 2026/27
findings.detail: The baseline has been "more accurately matched" to anticipated 2026/27 actual figures. The council explicitly states: "there is unlikely to be any upside variance and hence growth in the business rates system. Due to this, the Council has not included any forecast growth within its budget for 2026/27." This removes a historic income source from budget assumptions.
findings.matters: A significant income assumption has been removed from the revenue budget. Any actual growth cannot offset other pressures, and the £24.18m business rates baseline is now a ceiling, not a floor with upside.
findings.figures: Business rates baseline £24.180m (NSDC 40% share); baseline funding level £3.873m; no growth budgeted
findings.quote: Due to this, the Council has not included any forecast growth within its budget for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 allocates the council only 95% income protection, not the higher 100% available to other authorities
findings.detail: The protection metric for this council is above 15%, placing it in the worse-protected category. Over the three-year settlement, the council will receive 95% of the post-reform revised 2025/26 Core Spending Power. The review represents the first funding distribution change since 2013-14 and will "result in more redistribution of funding within the sector than any other for at least the last 13 years."
findings.matters: A lender needs to know this council faces relative funding deterioration compared to better-protected authorities, with ongoing risk of further relative loss over the three-year settlement.
findings.figures: Protection metric above 15% (threshold for 95% vs 100% protection); 2026/27 Core Spending Power £20.424m vs £20.004m revised 2025/26
findings.quote: Eligibility for 95% income protection is determined where a Shire District has a protection metric of greater than 15%.

findings.headline: Arkwood Developments Ltd, a wholly owned council company, is forecasting a pre-tax loss of £77k.
findings.detail: The council exercises shareholder oversight of Arkwood through the Executive Shareholder Committee. The company 'progressed housing delivery with 89 homes completed and 149 plots commenced, but reported a forecast pre-tax loss of £77k, reflecting the need for continued focus on cost control and sales performance.' While modest, this loss demonstrates operational strain in a subsidiary dependent on market conditions.
findings.matters: Wholly owned subsidiaries are contingent liabilities. Arkwood's losses drain council resources and may require future capital injections or loan guarantees. Combined with outer-year funding gaps of £4.3-4.6m, this adds financial pressure to the council.
findings.figures: £77k forecast pre-tax loss, 89 homes completed, 149 plots commenced
findings.quote: Arkwood progressed housing delivery with 89 homes completed and 149 plots commenced, but reported a forecast pre-tax loss of £77k, reflecting the need for continued focus on cost control and sales performance.

findings.headline: Internal Audit identified Limited Assurance on Business Continuity, signalling weaknesses in resilience planning.
findings.detail: Of 13 internal audit reviews conducted in 2024/25, two received Limited Assurance ratings: Business Continuity and Equality, Diversity and Inclusion. The auditor notes this highlights 'weaknesses in resilience planning'. This suggests the council lacks adequate contingency arrangements to maintain service delivery and financial operations during a crisis.
findings.matters: A lender depends on the council's operational resilience. Weak business continuity planning means the council could be unable to collect revenues or meet payment obligations during a cyber attack, facility failure, or staffing emergency.
findings.figures: Of 13 reviews: 4 Substantial Assurance, 4 Reasonable, 2 Limited Assurance, 3 advisory
findings.quote: two areas—Business Continuity and Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI) —were rated Limited Assurance, highlighting weaknesses in resilience planning and inclusivity governance.

findings.headline: The council underspent its capital programme by £8.78m (27% of HRA capital spend) in 2024/25 due to timing and slippage.
findings.detail: On the capital side, spending was £32.936m 'with an £8.780 million underspend attributed to timing and slippage.' This material underspend signals that the council may struggle to execute its £149m capital programme on time, potentially affecting benefit realization and revenue generation timelines.
findings.matters: Capital delivery slippage delays when the council realizes income or benefits from investments and postpones when borrowing actually crystallizes. It also indicates project execution risk.
findings.figures: £32.936m spent, £8.780m underspend (26.7% of HRA capital spend)
findings.quote: On the capital side, £32.936 million was spent, with an £8.780 million underspend attributed to timing and slippage.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased 8.4% in 2024/25, showing growing reliance on borrowing for capital investment.
findings.detail: The council's CFR increased 8.4% in 2024/25, indicating 'a greater reliance on borrowing to fund capital investment'. The capital programme includes £81.8m in planned borrowing across General Fund and HRA over 2024/25-2027/28. The auditor specifically notes risks including 'dependency on borrowing (particularly within the HRA), reliance on external grants, and limited unallocated capital receipts'.
findings.matters: Increasing borrowing dependency while facing outer-year funding pressures limits financial flexibility. The specific flagging of HRA borrowing risk is concerning, as housing authorities have limited capacity to cut HRA services without legal consequences.
findings.figures: £23.457m capital expenditure 2024/25, 8.4% CFR increase, £81.8m planned borrowing, £149m total capital programme 2024/25-2027/28
findings.quote: The increase in the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) by 8.4% in 2024/25 indicates a greater reliance on borrowing to fund capital investment.

findings.headline: The council faces structural funding gaps of £4.3m and £4.6m in 2026/27 and 2027/28, dependent on delivering £8.843m in savings.
findings.detail: The council moved from a previously forecast shortfall of £1.627m to a 'fully funded position through to 2028/29', but only by identifying and committing to £8.843m in savings and mitigations. The MTFP still projects 'funding gaps of £4.3 million in 2026/27 and £4.6 million in 2027/28' which the auditor emphasizes 'underline the importance of delivering these measures and continuing to identify further efficiencies and income opportunities to maintain long-term sustainability.'
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council can meet its obligations. Structural gaps three years out mean the council must execute significant savings or secure additional income/borrowing. If these fail to materialize, the council's financial position deteriorates rapidly.
findings.figures: £1.627m (previous forecast shortfall), £8.843m (identified savings/mitigations), £4.3m (2026/27 gap), £4.6m (2027/28 gap)
findings.quote: projected funding gaps of £4.3 million in 2026/27 and £4.6 million in 2027/28 underline the importance of delivering these measures and continuing to identify further efficiencies and income opportunities to maintain long-term sustainability.

news_drafts.headline: 2027-28 is the final budget for Newark and Sherwood in its current form; the council will cease to exist as a separate entity from 2028-29
news_drafts.lead: For a lender, this signals uncertainty in governance and accountability from 2028-29. Financial performance and structural change create risk during a transition. Service plans and financial forecasts beyond 2027-28 rest on the new unitary's decisions, not…

news_drafts.headline: Pay award for 2026/27 remains unsettled with employees requesting significantly above the employer's 3.3% offer
news_drafts.lead: Salary costs are the largest budget item. A settlement above the provisioned rate would force deficit-funding or require mid-year service reductions. Conversely, if the offer is accepted, it signals employee dissatisfaction during a major restructure.

news_drafts.headline: Funding deficits of £2.897m emerging by 2029/30 under current spending and grant assumptions
news_drafts.lead: A £2.9m shortfall in the final year of the MTFP signals deteriorating grant funding and business rates. Even though the new unitary will assume responsibility, it indicates underlying income pressures that may carry forward into the merged authority.
